_comment: Curated database of food additives with regulatory status across markets. Sources: EFSA, FDA, FSSAI. This is the core knowledge base for ingredient flagging.

additives.title: Banned in EU, UK, Canada, Brazil
additives.explanation: Potassium bromate is used to strengthen bread dough and make it rise higher. It has been classified as a possible human carcinogen (cancer-causing). The EU banned it in 1990, but it is still legally used in India.

additives.title: Requires warning label in EU
additives.explanation: Tartrazine is an artificial yellow color. In the EU, products containing it must carry a warning: 'may have adverse effect on activity and attention in children'. Studies have linked it to hyperactivity in children. It is freely used in India without warnings.

additives.title: Requires warning label in EU
additives.explanation: Sunset Yellow is an artificial orange-yellow dye. Like Tartrazine, the EU requires a hyperactivity warning on products containing it. It is associated with allergic reactions in some people, especially those with aspirin sensitivity.

additives.title: Artificial color — banned in some countries
additives.explanation: Brilliant Blue is a synthetic blue dye. It is banned in Austria, Belgium, France, Germany, and Switzerland. While permitted in India and the US, it is purely cosmetic — it adds no nutritional value and exists only to make food look more appealing.

additives.title: Banned in USA, Norway, Sweden
additives.explanation: Carmoisine is a red artificial dye. It is banned in the United States, Norway, and Sweden due to concerns about allergic reactions and hyperactivity in children. It is commonly found in Indian sweets and snacks.

additives.title: Possible carcinogen — restricted in EU
additives.explanation: BHA is a preservative used to prevent fats and oils from going rancid. The US National Toxicology Program classifies it as 'reasonably anticipated to be a human carcinogen'. The EU limits its use, but India allows it in many food categories.
additives.source: NTP 15th Report on Carcinogens; EU Regulation 1333/2008

additives.title: Restricted in several countries
additives.explanation: BHT is an antioxidant preservative similar to BHA. It is banned in Japan, Romania, Sweden, and Australia for food use. Some studies suggest links to liver and kidney damage at high doses. It is commonly used in Indian packaged foods.

additives.title: Source of artificial trans fats — banned by WHO
additives.explanation: Partially hydrogenated oils are the main source of artificial trans fats. The WHO called for a global ban on them by 2023. Trans fats increase bad cholesterol (LDL), decrease good cholesterol (HDL), and significantly raise heart disease risk. Even if the nutrition label says '0g trans fat', it can still contain up to 0.5g per serving (a legal loophole). If you see this in the ingredients, the product contains trans fats.
additives.source: WHO REPLACE initiative; FDA ban (2018); FSSAI limit: 2% of fat

additives.title: Forms benzene when combined with Vitamin C
additives.explanation: Sodium benzoate itself is relatively safe in small amounts. BUT when combined with ascorbic acid (Vitamin C), it can form benzene — a known carcinogen. If you see both sodium benzoate AND citric acid/ascorbic acid in the same product's ingredients, that is a genuine concern.

additives.title: Classified as 'possibly carcinogenic' by WHO (2023)
additives.explanation: Aspartame is an artificial sweetener ~200x sweeter than sugar. In 2023, the WHO's IARC classified it as 'possibly carcinogenic to humans' (Group 2B). However, the JECFA (another WHO body) maintained that it is safe within daily limits. The controversy is ongoing. It is commonly found in Indian 'sugar-free' and 'diet' products.
additives.source: IARC Group 2B classification (2023); JECFA ADI: 40mg/kg body weight

additives.title: Flavor enhancer — safe but often undisclosed
additives.explanation: MSG is a flavor enhancer that makes food taste more savory (umami). Despite decades of controversy, major food safety bodies consider it safe. The real concern: it can make processed food taste much better than it should, encouraging overconsumption. Also watch for hidden names like 'hydrolyzed vegetable protein', 'yeast extract', or 'natural flavoring' which contain free glutamate.
additives.source: FDA GRAS; EFSA ADI: 30mg/kg body weight

additives.title: Restricted in Japan and some EU countries
additives.explanation: TBHQ is a synthetic preservative used in oils and fats. In high doses, animal studies showed stomach tumors. It is banned in Japan and its use is restricted in several EU countries. It is commonly found in Indian fried snacks and instant noodles.

additives.title: Linked to obesity and metabolic issues
additives.explanation: HFCS is a cheap liquid sweetener made from corn starch. It is metabolized differently from regular sugar — it goes directly to the liver and is more likely to be converted to fat. It is strongly linked to obesity, fatty liver disease, and type 2 diabetes. Not common in Indian products yet, but increasingly appearing in imported/western-style foods.
additives.source: Multiple peer-reviewed studies; American Journal of Clinical Nutrition

additives.title: High in saturated fat — most common cooking oil in Indian packaged food
additives.explanation: Palm oil is not toxic or banned anywhere, but it is very high in saturated fat (50%). Most Indian packaged snacks use it because it is the cheapest cooking oil. If a product says 'vegetable oil' without specifying which one, it is almost certainly palm oil. It is worse than mustard oil, olive oil, or groundnut oil for heart health, but better than partially hydrogenated oils.

additives.title: Natural coloring — generally safe
additives.explanation: Annatto is a natural orange-red color derived from seeds of the achiote tree. It is generally considered safe and is a much better choice than artificial colors. If you see this instead of tartrazine or sunset yellow, it is a positive sign.

additives.title: Controversial thickener — some concerns about gut inflammation
additives.explanation: Carrageenan is a natural thickener extracted from seaweed, commonly used in dairy alternatives (almond milk, soy milk) and processed foods. Some studies suggest it may cause gut inflammation. The EU considered banning it from infant formula. It is still generally considered safe by most regulators.
additives.source: EFSA re-evaluation; various studies on gut inflammation

additives.title: Artificial sweetener — limited long-term data
additives.explanation: Acesulfame K is an artificial sweetener often combined with aspartame or sucralose. It is 200x sweeter than sugar. Current evidence suggests it is safe within limits, but some researchers argue that long-term studies are insufficient. Commonly found in Indian 'sugar-free' drinks and supplements.
additives.source: EFSA ADI: 9mg/kg body weight; FDA GRAS

additives.title: Linked to cancer risk in processed meats
additives.explanation: Sodium nitrite is used as a preservative in processed meats (sausages, bacon, ham, salami). When heated at high temperatures, nitrites can form nitrosamines — which are known carcinogens. The WHO classified processed meat as a Group 1 carcinogen, and nitrites are a major reason why.

misleading_terms.reality: The word 'natural' here is misleading. 'Natural flavoring' can be heavily processed and chemically altered. It just means the original source was natural — the final product may be far from it. By regulation, it only needs to have a natural origin, not be natural in the way consumers understand it.

'Multigrain' just means more than one grain was used. It does NOT mean whole grain. The grains could all be refined (stripped of fiber and nutrients). Look for 'whole wheat' or 'whole grain' as the FIRST ingredient instead.

'No added sugar' does not mean low sugar. The product may contain natural sugars (from fruit juice concentrate, honey, dates) that are just as caloric. Check the total sugar content in the nutrition table.
'Baked not fried' sounds healthier but baked snacks often compensate with more fat, salt, or sugar to match the taste of fried ones. Always check the actual fat and sodium content.
This could mean as little as 1-2% fruit content, often as fruit juice concentrate (which is basically sugar). The rest could be water, sugar, artificial flavors, and colors.

'Light' or 'Lite' has no standardized legal definition in India. It might mean lighter in color, taste, texture — or nothing specific at all. In the US/EU, 'light' must mean 30% less of something (calories, fat), but in India this is not enforced.

All plant-based oils are naturally cholesterol-free (cholesterol only exists in animal products). So labeling vegetable oil as 'cholesterol free' is technically true but intentionally misleading — it implies a special health benefit that every plant oil already has.

'Enriched' means nutrients were added back after processing removed them. 'Fortified' means nutrients were added that were never there. Both suggest the original food was processed enough to need artificial supplementation. Whole foods don't need enrichment.

Many 'protein chips' have only marginally more protein than regular chips (e.g., 5g vs 3g per serving) but are marketed at 2-3x the price. Always check the actual protein per 100g and compare with the price.
